Hi, I built a small prototype for automated theory construction over equational problems using Lean.
It runs a loop:

  • pick a conjecture
  • try proof / counterexample
  • verify in Lean
  • accumulate theorems in a shared file
    So it gradually grows a lemma base (Derived.lean) and reuses it.
    The system is orchestrator + LLM worker (Codex CLI).
    It's still a minimal prototype, but already runs end-to-end.
    I'm particularly interested in whether a nontrivial theory can emerge automatically from a small set of axioms.
    Any feedback would be very appreciated.
    Repo: https://github.com/tukamilano/automated-theory-construction-lean

Thanks! I'm currently improving the prompts and running a new batch.
In the meantime, here are a few small examples from the current version:

I also attached a longer run (~5h) from an earlier version.
The new run should be cleaner (less trivial lemmas, better reuse).
I'll share updated results once it's done.

theorem thm_op_000015 : ∀ {α : Type u} [Nontrivial α], ∃ _ : SemigroupLike01 α, ¬ Subsingleton α := by
  intro α _
  letI : SemigroupLike01 α :=
    { mul := fun x _ => x
      ax_left_idempotent := by
        intro x
        rfl
      ax_right_absorb_duplicate := by
        intro x y
        rfl
      ax_middle_swap := by
        intro x y z
        rfl }
  refine ⟨inferInstance, ?_⟩
  exact not_subsingleton α


theorem thm_op_000016 : ∀ α : Type u, ∃ _ : SemigroupLike01 α, ∀ x y : α, x * y = x := by
  intro α
  letI : SemigroupLike01 α :=
    { mul := fun x _ => x
      ax_left_idempotent := by
        intro x
        rfl
      ax_right_absorb_duplicate := by
        intro x y
        rfl
      ax_middle_swap := by
        intro x y z
        rfl }
  refine ⟨inferInstance, ?_⟩
  intro x y
  rfl


theorem thm_op_000003_is_false : ¬(∀ {α : Type u} [SemigroupLike01 α], ∃ e : α, ∀ x : α, e * x = x ∧ x * e = x) := by
  intro h
  let α : Type u := ULift.{u} PEmpty
  letI : SemigroupLike01 α :=
    { mul := fun x _ => PEmpty.elim x.down
      ax_left_idempotent := by
        intro x
        exact PEmpty.elim x.down
      ax_right_absorb_duplicate := by
        intro x y
        exact PEmpty.elim x.down
      ax_middle_swap := by
        intro x y z
        exact PEmpty.elim x.down }
  obtain ⟨e, _⟩ := h (α := α)
  exact PEmpty.elim e.down

These are the theorems obtained after running the system for about six hours.
https://github.com/tukamilano/automated-theory-construction-lean/blob/main/AutomatedTheoryConstruction/Derived.lean

My goal is to automatically generate as much generalization and structure beyond the internal language as possible.
Thank you for a feedback. I updated README and attach some examples

I wrote a blog post presenting a result in provability theory.

If possible, I would appreciate feedback on the generated results.
Also, if there are other small-scale systems—such as in logic or language theory—that would be suitable to experiment with, I would be grateful for your suggestions.

I generated code to explore some properties of provability logic and the type system λU⁻, and attempted to compare the quality of the resulting files with that of Basic.lean in mathlib though there seems to be a large gap.
The main problem is that the system progresses fully automatically, making it difficult for the developer to keep track of what is happening and to evaluate the results.

Small update on automated theory construction in Lean:

I applied the exploration loop to a minimal axiom system for canonical commutation relations (creation/annihilation operators + vacuum axiom).

From this setup, the system generated and verified a family of structural results about the span of iterated creation operators.

Example (formal Lean statement):

/-- The Fock span is canonically linearly equivalent to the polynomial representation via creation-operator evaluation on the vacuum. -/
theorem main_thm_fock_span_linear_equiv_polynomial : ∀ {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V] (bc : BosonCore V), bc.vacuum ≠ 0 → ∃ Φ : Polynomial ℂ ≃ₗ[ℂ] Submodule.span ℂ (Set.range bc.ket), ∀ p : Polynomial ℂ, (Φ p : V) = (Polynomial.aeval bc.aDagger p) bc.vacuum := by
  intro V _ _ bc hvac
  have hli : LinearIndependent ℂ (fun n : ℕ => bc.ket n) :=
    thm_ket_linear_independent_of_vacuum_ne_zero_000006 (bc := bc) hvac
  refine ⟨(Polynomial.toFinsuppIsoLinear ℂ).trans hli.linearCombinationEquiv, ?_⟩
  intro p
  change (Finsupp.linearCombination ℂ (fun n : ℕ => bc.ket n) (Polynomial.toFinsupp p) : V) =
    (Polynomial.aeval bc.aDagger p) bc.vacuum
  rw [Finsupp.linearCombination_apply]
  simpa [Polynomial.sum_def, Finsupp.sum, Polynomial.support_toFinsupp,
    Polynomial.toFinsupp_apply] using
    (thm_aeval_a_dagger_vacuum_support_sum_000060 (bc := bc) p).symm
  • The system recovers structure analogous to a polynomial representation via the creation operator acting on the vacuum.
  • Similar behavior has been observed across different axiom systems, although the generated results vary in form.
  • Although this experiment starts from a minimal axiom system, the loop does not fundamentally rely on axioms alone; in practice, it can also be applied to partially specified theory fragments or existing formal developments.

Interested in what kinds of domains or axiom systems this approach might generalize to in practice.

Hi Kei, I am also interested in exploring what can be accomplished with fully autonomous development.

I've been building a system that does something similar with multiple specialized Claude agents running concurrently.

So far this system has produced 1500 proof files. Research problems go through an iterate-and-branch pattern where proving one theorem often surfaces open sub-questions that get added back to the queue.

The gallery is at https://leangenius.org. (inspired by the "rap genius" website where rap lyrics are annotated by experts)

the system progresses fully automatically, making it difficult to keep track of what is happening

I am trying to control hallucination and overstated progress with dedicated auditor and peer-review agents that independently check outputs - I imagine you will need similar "critical feedback" stages in your pipeline.

How are you seeding topics into your system? Have you seen anything genuinely surprising come out yet?

Thank you for your interest.
I was very impressed that your system has already produced 1500 proof files. The iterate-and-branch method also feels very close to my own approach.

  • Seeding Strategy

Regarding how I seed topics, I currently define this explicitly via prompts as an “open problem expansion” process.
More concretely, I use prompts such as new_problem_expander to generate new subproblems from existing open problems, allowing outputs in both natural language and Lean code.
In addition, the step that converts generated statements into well-formed Lean propositions is separated from the prover itself, and I include a repair stage when the syntax is invalid.
I generate seeds by expanding both reference documents and Lean code containing the core definitions into new open problems via prompts.

  • On “Surprising” Results

To be honest, I find it difficult at this stage to evaluate whether the results are genuinely surprising.
In unexplored domains, it is hard to assess novelty without sufficient domain expertise.
That said, I have observed some interesting behaviors.
For example, in experiments on provability logic, the system generates patterns where the existence of Gödel fixed points aligns with certain equivalence relations, as well as counterexample-like behavior where Henkin fixed points do not follow from Gödel fixed points under APS alone.
While I cannot yet determine whether these are genuinely new results, I do find it encouraging that nontrivial relationships reflecting the internal structure of the system are emerging automatically.
On the other hand, the current search process is biased toward something like “Basic.lean-style” lemma accumulation, so it is not particularly optimized for producing clearly surprising results. I expect more structural results may emerge after sufficient accumulation.
At the moment, the main bottleneck seems to be evaluation rather than generation.

I would be very interested in how you are handling evaluation on your side.

Yes, generating data is much easier than evaluating it! I'm probably at a worse disadvantage than you because I am also an amateur at the math (with the usual physicist hubris to think that I'll be able to make a useful contribution!) -- but I do think that we should be able to create pipelines that minimize the garbage out. I don't think I have a better idea here beyond repeatedly "review and revise" until the agents are satisfied. It does seem to be helpful to have multiple gate checks that each focus on particular problems. Exaggerated claims of novelty or usefulness seem to be a big problem (general ai sycophancy) An agent will prove a trivial supporting lemma and describe it as an advance. Or it will axiomatize the hard part of a theorem and claim the result is verified. Having dedicated skeptical agents that specifically look for overclaiming has helped, but it's an ongoing battle.

To answer your question about evaluation more directly... I have a "seeker" agent that proposes research problems by surveying the existing gallery for gaps and cross-referencing with known open problem lists (I collected all the Erdős problems and a few other lists I found so that has been the starting point). I don't have a good solution for evaluating genuine mathematical novelty beyond automated google search...

I've also been submitting work to Aristotle but not really getting much beyond what Codex or Claude can do - I am still trying to figure out how to use it effectively in an automated way. I expect some sort of automated research program will eventually produce new math but clearly we have along way to go.

Thank you for the link - I am going to adopt some of your anti-sycophancy criteria and add a periodic "synthesis scan" agent that reviews recent work and attempts to combine into something more structural. This is the main_theorem_suggester concept from your code.

Hi! I'm thinking of creating a tutorial on building a minimal Lean4 autoformalizer from scratch - something like a stripped-down version of current systems - to help people understand how these tools actually work under the hood.

Would this be a useful gap to fill? Are there specific concepts or failure modes you'd want addressed for someone entering the field? I'd love a pointer if something similar already exists.

Personally, I think it’s also important to make explicit why a definition is introduced in a particular way, since otherwise it’s easy to end up with statements that type-check but don’t match the intended semantics.

This is mainly fruitless. If it were to find "new" math, it would be covered by heaps of noise and no expert would want to invest time, if it is just a supposedly new "theory" or something like that.

There is also "new" math in the Library of Babel, but it is just drowned in endless noise. I would suggest anchoring them with solving a open problem (with a known correct statement), and they can then devise "new" math / theory for trying to solve that problem, but in the end they will need to solve the problems to show that their advances / theories are worth of taking a look at. You can for example get some problems from Formal Conjectures.

That would be a much better token dump and is closer to how mathematicians find / create new theories (see preface of Erdos Problem Website).

Thank you for your thoughtful comments.

new math would be covered by heaps of noise

I agree that noise is a serious issue.
My current view is that simple duplication or shallow variants can be reduced by refactoring and filtering. However, I also recognize that this alone is not sufficient — the harder problem is identifying which results are actually meaningful or useful.
I also think this difficulty is not unique to automated systems: even for humans, judging the value of mathematical results is often challenging, especially outside one’s area of expertise. This becomes even more critical in automated settings due to the scale of generated results.

no expert would want to invest time

I agree that this is a real concern.
One possible use case I have in mind is not to present outputs directly as "new theorems" for experts to evaluate, but rather to use the system as an exploratory tool.
For example, when introducing a new definition, structure, or set of assumptions, the system could help map out local properties and candidate relationships around it. This could provide a kind of "landscape view" of the theory, which might assist intuition-building.
In that sense, the goal is closer to supporting exploration than producing immediately publishable results.

anchor with solving an open problem

I find the idea of anchoring to open problems quite compelling, and I agree that it provides a clear evaluation signal.
At the same time, I think there are two slightly different modes of operation:

  • Goal-driven exploration (e.g., solving a specific conjecture)
  • Open-ended exploration (e.g., expanding consequences of definitions or assumptions via generalization or variation)
    My current system is closer to the latter.
    However, I agree that incorporating goal-oriented signals could help guide the search and make the results more meaningful. A possible direction is to combine both modes, where open-ended exploration generates structure, and goal-driven components help prioritize or evaluate it.

Thank you again for the insightful feedback.

I have opined on theory-building on MathOverflow. Much of that advice is too vague to be of use to machines at the present time, but in addition to the "anchoring to open problems" suggestion above, one test of the utility of a new theory is whether it provides better proofs of existing theorems. "Better" is not easy to quantify, but "shorter" could act as a first approximation.

I'm not sure how useful this idea is, though. My guess is that the current state of the art is rather far away from being able to formulate new theories that dramatically simplify and illuminate large and well-established chunks of existing mathematics.

Thank you.
I feel that, when reconstructing the set of propositions obtained through exploration, it is necessary to consider ways of organizing them in a more structural manner.
In particular, the extent to which we can simplify proofs of existing theorems — for example, in terms of proof length or structure — seems like a useful criterion for evaluating the utility of the results.
